Lazarsfeld and Friedman introduced the concept of symplectic modifications in 1990, providing a novel definition of rational maps that are compatible with symplectic structure. They proposed a conjecture asserting that every proper symplectic morphism is essentially a composition of blow-ups and inverse transformations of divisors that preserve the symplectic form. This paper aims to extend the framework of symplectic modifications and explore the proposed Lazarsfeld and Friedman conjecture from a different perspective. We define a class of maps known as proper symplectic transformations and demonstrate that, in the context of these maps, any proper symplectic morphism can be realized as a sequence of blow-ups and inverse transformations of divitors that maintain the symplectic form.

Transplanting kidneys that don't perfectly match with a patient's body has become an increasing norm, yet measuring how well they're compatible is quite complicated. The compatibility is complicated further by its inherently social nature and the lack of a clear standard for compatibility. This research presents a fresh perspective on compatibility, framing it in the context of rational choice and social coordination, complicating it further by considering the gradual nature of compatibility changes. The resulting mathematical model provides the framework for assessing the degree of willingness of a patient to accept an incompatible kidney, from which the priority for listing such kidneys can be derived. The derived principles can guide the development of policies for kidney transplantation.

We investigate the efficacy of a variety of unsupervised and supervised techniques in
capturing the Loughran-McDonald (LM) word polarity vectors for the task of
financial text sentiment analysis. We discover that even enhanced semantic
spaces, such as those utilizing the ComSkipBigPram model, fail to accurately
represent the original LM polarities when employed in supervised sentiment
classification tasks. We further examine the ComSkipGram model's representations
and determine that the original LM polarities contain valuable information not
already encoded in the semantic space. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that
the temporal evolution of the representation of a single stock with high
polarizability can be effectively captured and that the magnitude of a stock's
sentiment change is correlated with the polarizability of its associated text.

This paper extends the waveform optimization framework from integrated data and power transmission to SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems, converting their complex matrix structures into simpler OFDM equivalents. This facilitates the application of efficient OFDM hardware for these systems.

This research examines the impact of solidification and liquid phase transitions on buried interfaces within a one-dimensional, powder bed environment. The analysis takes into account latent heat effects and heat loss to the surrounding environment through radiative transfer. The study's mathematical model is numerically solved using an innovative hybrid method that combines the mixed level-set / embedded boundary technique. This method leverages the benefits of both level-set and embedded boundary approaches while minimizing their respective limitations. The mixed method utilizes the capability of level-set approaches to effectively track multiple interfaces, along with the benefit of embedded boundary approaches in integrating source terms within the numerical integrator. The method demonstrates high accuracy in area preservation and geometric representation, with minimal time-step restrictions. The technique is validated through the analysis of a powder bed environment, revealing how interface interactions can minimize external interface movement and maximize internal interface movement as a result. The current method is limited to one-dimensional settings; however, its development for multidimensional environments remains an open area of research.

In the context of multi-player games, having a rationalizable equilibrium as a foundation is essential for effective strategy learning algorithms. Although current learning algorithms can secure average rationalizability in single-player games, achieving a sum of rationalizability guarantees in multi-player games remains a challenging prospect. This study develops learning algorithms that achieve a multi-player setting with rationalizability guarantees of $O(\log T / \log \log T)$ in the full information scenario and a $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{K \log (T/K)})$ in the bandit scenario, where T denotes the total rounds and K denotes the count of available actions. These results are the first instances of learning algorithms capable of ensuring a combined rationalizability equilibrium across all players in multi-player games.

In large-scale networks, an outbreak can paralyze critical services rapidly, posing a severe threat to public health and economic stability. To mitigate this risk, a new strategy has been proposed that leverages the ability to rewire network connections for protection, allowing a portion of the network nodes to switch to a safer, isolated sub-network. This paper holder 's theorem, derived from an extensive SIR model of a dynamically rewired network, demonstrates how the network can be structured to prevent complete node infection. However, when the isolation of infected nodes is taken into account, the theorem's limitations become apparent, restricting its practical applicability under certain infection rate conditions. To navigate these limitations, the research proposes two alternative network designs that can significantly delay the inevitable infection of the entire network, providing valuable insights for creating resilient networks in the face of epidemics.

This paper presents a unified approach to describing PDF reweighting and retraining,Re-shuffling and tuning individually for various entities including probability density functions (PDFs), observables, processes, and data. We propose a consistent methodology based on the reweighting algorithm developed by Schmidt and due Toellner, which leverages the likelihood object from existing processes and employs a neural network-based classifier for others. This framework enables users to manage and analyze PDF uncertainties, process uncertainties, and training set biases using the existing due Toellner framework and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO. It also facilitates the study of individual instances, which is indispensable for interpreting final results.

Reinforcement learning agents quickly learn skills by remembering and reviewing past experiences, similar to how humans and animals adapt to new situations. In complex tasks for artificial intelligence, a simple memory system, known as experience replay, allows the agent to enhance its knowledge efficiently. However, traditional experience replay memory stores past experiences without considering their importance, treating diverse experiences the same way. This paper proposes a new approach, called Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VD-ELE), which dynamically prioritizes experiences based on their variability and importance. By adapting the storage and review process, the VD-ELE memory management strategy enables a Policy Enhancement outcome. The proposed method has been tested on complex tasks using deep neural networks, demonstrating its effectiveness in comparing and outperforming existing techniques.

In the realm of human-human conversations, each exchange can lead to multiple, vastly different directions based on responding statements that differ even in their fundamental categories. To replicate these complex and divergent conversations, current dialogue models typically follow a uniform approach to data processing and model architecture, limiting their effectiveness. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel framework called MultiTalk, which emulates the infinite-branching potential of real-world conversations by adapting both the data handling process and the model structure in response to the diversity of dialogue content. At the data handling stage, a responsive statement that leads to an infinite sequence of conversations, we employ a dynamic text operation that adjusts the word embedding of the statement in real-time. Similarly, we apply a modular architecture with adaptable components that reflect the richness of the conversation content at the model structure stage. As a result of these innovations, our model outperforms the state-of-the-art in predicting the next sentence in a conversation, particularly in terms of accuracy and temporal information.

We introduce a novel technique for rapidly simulating the dynamics of large N bodies in gravitational systems based on modified theories. Our method allows for n body simulations of a specific model, N(f), within the no-scale dark matter chameleon framework, where a coupling parameter is set to zero. By utilizing a redefined phase space with appropriately transformed variables, N body equations of motion are solved in a computationally efficient manner. Our algorithm enables a million particle simulation at a cost comparable to a hundred thousand particle simulation, achieving this speedup while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Our technique for efficiently simulating N bodies in modified gravitational theories opens up a broader range of cosmological and astrophysical scenarios for investigation.

The connection between multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) and Gaussian free field (GFQ) was initially established by Miller and Sheffield in a groundbreaking study. This paper deepens and extends that connection by specifically examining multiple SLEs in the context of a two-dimensional plane. It demonstrates that the trajectories of multiple SLEs can be directly attributed to the driving particles of a one-particle random log-gas. Furthermore, it reveals that the driving particles of the SLEs and the SLE trajectories themselves are independent with respect to the GFQ.

In today's fast-paced work environments, collaborative knowledge creation and
documentation are essential yet challenging processes. This challenge is compounded
by the need to incorporate technical details that often demand a high level of
expertise. Our new tool, WorkingWiki, is a介维Wiki platform with significant customization
options, designed specifically for advanced collaborative projects. It features a
tailored MediaWiki structure comprising sections for core knowledge, recent changes,
a code repository interface, an interactive projection of ongoing work, and a
dedicated editor. Our pilot project, a high-level documentation of a cutting-edge and
complex decoding method for mental images, has utilized our platform so far.

This research paper examines the reaction of a turbulent jet fire in a linearized framework when subjected to external acoustic vibrations. The goal is to model the flame's response using a simplified mathematical approach. To achieve this, an Active Flame Method is applied to transform non-linear equations into linear equations that describe the flame's structure. Various excitation scenarios are tested to determine how the jet fire reacts acoustically. The results are analyzed using stability concepts from control theory, showcasing a clear understanding of damped oscillations, over-damped, and unstable responses. The study reveals that the jet fire behaves like a weakly stable structure, exhibiting amplified responses to certain frequencies due to its inherent dynamics. The method's effectiveness in modeling and predicting jet fire reactions is demonstrated, providing a actionable framework for designing flame suppression or stabilization systems.

The investigation of neutrino mass through the $0\nu\beta\beta$ process and the analysis of diverse astrophysical processes necessitate an in-depth neutrino-everything theory. 
In the context of the ultralight dark matter field that is influenced by the neutrino effective mass, we establish a novel mechanism for the neutron excess generation within neutron stars and demonstrate how this process can lead to the suppression of $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay probability in extreme environments like core collapse. 
As an initial step, the necessary theoretical framework is presented to facilitate subsequent, more detailed studies of such scenarios. 
Moreover, the magnitude and temporal variation of the neutrino-induced dark matter signal can be calculated and mapped for a particular experiment, serving as a case study for such investigations. 
This study aims to provide a starting point for the design of detectors capable of simultaneously measuring $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay and the dark matter signal, thereby enabling significant advancements in our comprehension of the absolute scale of the neutrino mass.

Nonlocal gravitation theory postulates that for any given source, there are an infinite number of possible constitutive connections, including the well-known metric connection, which ensures the nonlocal general relativity reduces to the metric version. A shift from the metric connection necessitates calculating essential parts of the connection, referred to as essential tetrads, derived from the source, connection, and a specific metric that is determined by the constitutive connection. The paper explores the reduction of nonlocal general relativity to the metric theory, demonstrating the calculation of essential tetrads, and discusses some of its physical implications.

This study aims to synpose and compare the results from GWAS studies conducted by two independent groups on 18 human traits across the UCSC Genome Browser. Human traits were selected based on associated genes identified through functional genomics experiments, specifically Chromia analysis of data from DNase-seq, H3K36me3, H3K4me3, H3K27ac, and peak calls for ATAC-seq on the human genome. Two independent research teams have mapped over a hundred genes associated with various human characteristics through GWAS studies of the human genome, with significant contributions from functional genomics research. We have systematically evaluated and compared the results from these two studies as part of our effort to enhance the applicability of functional genomic research, specifically Chromia, in analyzing and integrating annotations for the UCSC Genome Browser. We found substantial overlap in results from these studies, with 15 out of 18 characteristics showing consistent results across both studies. Notable examples of shared results include the WNT5A and DCC genes associated with nerve traits, FGF5 gene associated with hair traits, IL10 gene associated with immune system traits, EDAR gene associated with mouth traits as well as hair traits, and MSX1 gene that is associated with teeth traits as well as mouth traits. However, there was a discrepancy in results for eye traits, with different associated genes identified by the two studies.

In recent years, research into tiny systems produced in lead-lead collisions at the LHC has been fueled by interesting observations. Initially considered marginal, these systems have been found to yield data that is highly valuable for interpreting larger collisions involving nuclei. This article explores various tiny systems, including proton-proton, ion-proton, and forwardly boosted systems, and discusses several critical aspects of analyzing tiny systems. It highlights several underutilized features of PbPb data, such as flow in two-particle correlations, quark yield measurements, and jet modifications in nuclear matter.

Using a semi-empirical approach, we calculated the recurrence times for 41 transient X-ray binary systems in the Milky Way's center by analyzing their light curves from the SWIFT archive. These calculations consider the initial rotation period and decay rate of X-ray bursts for each system. We found that most of these systems have recurrence times between 0.5 and 3 years, with a typical value of around 1 year. When compared with observed recurrence times from various studies, our results closely match the reported intervals for specific systems in the Milky Way's center. Furthermore, by correlating recurrence times with the amplitude of X-ray burst recoveries, we characterized the currently dormant X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center. Some systems with short recurrence times and high burst recovery amplitudes are likely in a recycling stage, while others with long recurrence times and low burst recovery amplitudes are considered failed binary systems.

In this paper, a theoretical framework is developed to delve into the nature of "momentum sidebands" in solid-state systems. These are sidebands observed in the context of a specific quantum state, characterized by vibrational frequencies and amplitude, in conjunction with an electron's spin precession frequency and phase. The analysis pertains to the impact of periodic lattice movements on various electron properties and phases, as well as on the definition and expression of spin-vibrational and electron-vibrational interactions. These interactions are shown to be proportional to the amplitude of lattice motion and influenced by a particular momentum operator that can either generate or destroy a vibrational quantum. The theoretical findings are then applied to the demonstration of new entanglement and superposition states, involving the electron's momentum, spin, and interaction with phonons.

In the Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, determining the relationship between a sentence pair is a fundamental capability for understanding human language. However, the standard NLI data sets fail to capture more complex aspects of language, including discourse relationships and semantic diversity within a single sentence. We investigate the underrepresented diversity of natural language inference labels in the open-access STARS NLI dataset by visually analyzing the underlying concept classifications of hundreds of sentences that are labeled as "contradictions". Our manual study reveals an overrepresentation of discourse contradictions compared to other concept categories. Consequently, we identify the potential for standard NLI to contradict its annotations and the necessity of explicitly annotating discourse relationships in NLI datasets. We further examine the challenges and opportunities presented by such contradictions for state-of-the-art neural networks and propose a novel enhancement to existing NLI models incorporating tactical semantic variety awareness. Our model achieves superior performance in predicting natural language inference relationships when evaluated against the STARS NLI dataset.

Our numerical models of rotating substellar bodies beyond the point of zero angular velocity have now been achieved.
Using a scale-based noise reduction technique, we processed $10^{-3} \rm erg$ numerical data from $100$ simulations, covering an extensive range of rotation rates and masses from $0.01$ to $10$ Earth masses.
The relationships between rotating and non-rotating figures have been determined for objects with varying masses and speeds through visualized scatter plots, with theoretical limit lines indicating the range of stability.
Fitting formulas for the radii of rotating substellar bodies in the context of the Baraffe et al. (2001) model have been derived, as well as non-dimensional expressions for the radii differences between rotating and non-rotating bodies.
Indicative scatter patterns have been identified that may aid in distinguishing between substellar bodies and planets in future observational studies.

This research explores efficient methods for incorporating the effects of
external particles into calculations of scattering processes, which are used
in precision analysis at particle accelerators. We compare multiple ways to
conclude such calculations and discover that using effective operators for the
production of single photons and gluons can offer significant improvements - up
to a few percent for qQbar annihilation processes and around 1% for QQbar
annihilation processes - when calculating cross-sections at next-to-leading order
in quantum chromodynamics. We observe that the effective operators for single
gluon production achieve their highest precision near the threshold for producing
particles, but this is not always reflected in actual scattering processes. We
also examine an alternative method of incorporating the effects of external
particles, which involves using modified parton distribution functions. We
propose that these modifications can be interpreted as effective operators and
show that using them in conjunction with NLO calculations can also provide
accurate results. We provide access to all code utilized in this analysis on
GitHub.

The particle nature of afterglows from gamma-ray bursts is explained by the interaction of relativistic outflows with their surrounding ambient medium. As these outflows decelerate, the spectral features shift into the energy ranges detectable by optical and X-ray instruments. Due to the constant evolution of physical parameters, the observations can only be made meaningful through detailed theoretical models of afterglows. These models, although numerous and intricate, are hard to interpret and compare. A potential solution to this issue is a simple, universal way to represent the findings, allowing for an in-depth exploration of the data.

It is shown through a proof that is both parameterized and constructive that, given a graph G and an integer k, the graph can be split into two disjoint parts X and Y, with the following properties: the subgraph formed by the edges between X and Y, denoted as $X\boxtimes Y$, is edgeless, and the subgraphs formed by the edges within X and Y, denoted as $G[X]$ and $G[Y]$, have maximum degrees no greater than k. This method allows for the determination of the maximum degree bound in terms of list coloring, as well as other related parameters, in a way that is efficiently computable.

This research proposes an integrated approach that combines two key areas, assisted gaits for robust performance in legged creatures and enhanced energy management in two-legged walkers, to develop a more energy-efficient and resilient humanoid walker. A new, fully actuated bipedal gait is presented, featuring a flight phase where both legs are ungrounded, and developed through a modified passivity control method. This assisted gait enables the walker to recover from falls, avoid obstacles, and absorb external shocks, all while using simple and energy-saving operations. A novel, real-time energy-optimization strategy is also introduced to maximize the walker's ability to use its energy storage systems effectively, considering variations in ground conditions and load conditions. A resilient, assisted three-hurdle passage is studied as part of this approach, where the walker clears obstacles at ground level, in the air, and above its head, all while maintaining energy efficiency. It is shown that this method of passage allows the walker to clear taller obstacles compared to when both feet are on the ground, all while using the same amount of energy. Despite showing promising results, the usage of a energy-storage system like a flywheel in bipedal walkers is untested, all while the combination of a air-assisted flight phase and energy-optimization strategy to clear obstacles, at the cost of increased mechanical complexity, is also untested.

Let K be a local field extended with p-root unity for a prime number p not equal to the characteristic of K, and F be a respected field contained within K. A completed residue map is said to be achieved by F if it satisfies the property that K as a vector space over F is spanned by Teichmüller lifts of a basis of the residue field of K over the residue field of F. We establish that if the residue field of K over F has a finite degree, then the respected field F undoubtedly realizes a finite dimension. Conversely, if F has a infinite dimension, then the residue field of K over F is shown to be transcendental over the residue field of F. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm for identifying the respected subfield of K(\zeta_p) over F_q that has the residue field of K over F as its exact degree, along with generating a basis of F over the residue field of F.

In response to security threats like DoS and side-channel attacks, frequency scaling has been employed to slow down processors and mitigate risks, but research into the effects of changing the CPU's clock speed is restricted due to the technical difficulties in implementing such experiments. To address this limitation, a new tool called HyperDegrade was developed to readily modify CPU frequencies by bypassing firmware settings, enabling easier investigation of the impacts of frequency scaling on various aspects including programming, side-channel security, and cryptographic protocols. Despite the efficiency of this approach, it is not universally applicable and requires a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of the CPU's architecture, which could lead to an unintended exposure of sensitive data to side-channel leaks.

This note presents a novel unknotting strategy applicable to traditional and welded links, surpassing previously reported methods. By demonstrating the inability of the fundamental identity and the welding identity to undermine this approach, we provide the underlying abstract idea.

We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher loop constitutes a Vassiliev characteristic starting at third order, and by examining certain invariants of immersed circles, we derive an expression for the minimal order of integration for this characteristic.

In the Multi-Agent Delivery Competition, autonomous delivery bots navigate a complex urban environment to deliver food orders, competing against other autonomous systems in a simulated version of Pittsburgh. This multi-agent delivery scenario encompasses a wide array of challenges drawn from multiple research fields, focusing particularly on a set of simulated network disruptions and the resulting tactical collaboration among multiple autonomous agents. Our research concentrates specifically on the design of a collaborative strategy for a constrained set of delivery agents, overcoming network disruptions that obstruct communication and cause data loss among the agents. Our strategy employs a predefined set of constrained communication protocols that change over time to convey the most crucial information, despite the intermittent nature of the network disruptions. Our set of designed strategy constraints draws inspiration from real-world applications of autonomous multi-agent systems, expanding upon a prior constrained computation and communication ability research project. Our approach involves a wide set of designed strategy combinations for an expanded fleet of agents in a more intricate environment, leveraging an agent-based modeling approach to evaluate a range of constrained communication protocols that enable a degree of purposeful team collaboration within the competition.

This paper examines the privacy implications of implementing a Federated Gradient Descent framework. We first analyze the conventional approach, in which clients participate by providing feedback to the system, and demonstrate that PGV can potentially reveal the entire trained model, thus breaching privacy protections. To address this issue, we propose two innovative protocols that employ artificial data to protect the integrity of the VRF protocol while preventing any leakage of sensitive information. Next, we investigate a second scenario where multiple servers collaborate to provide proof verification services, and show that the PGV attack can also uncover crucial secret keys utilized in their communication. To mitigate this risk, we develop two assault-c resistant schemes, along with corresponding cryptographic proofs of security. Both the devised protocols are practical and can be integrated into present implementations with minimal overhead.

The conventional kernel kernel estimation method relies on a kernel density estimator with the Epanechnikov kernel, which has limited performance due to its wide parameter range. This paper proposes an innovative alternative by leveraging the Fourier attributes of a kernel, enabling the estimation of a kernel based on data, and significantly reducing storage requirements. We illustrate the application of this concept with a simple yet effective algorithm for kernel estimation and compare its performance against the traditional kernel method and a neural network-based estimator. Furthermore, we develop two advanced versions of this algorithm and conduct a comprehensive evaluation, showing that this pseudo-random approach offers a robust and efficient solution for kernel estimation.

We demonstrate that any abstract group can be embedded into the product of a simplicial complex known as a Garland. Using a revised staircase algorithm, we break down the simplicial complex into sectors that can be mapped via conformal equivalence. These sectors, being topologically spheres, simplify group embedding. This result builds on previous work by Jonsson and Smillie.

We prove a novel Möbius curvature inflexibility statement for compact conformally smooth hypersurfaces within the n+2 dimensional sphere, denoted as S^(n+2). Specifically, a conformally smooth hypersurface, denoted as M, in the n+2 dimensional sphere, denoted as S^(n+2), is shown to have a sequence of points on its scalar curvature function that are greater than a positive constant, denoted as $\epsilon$, which is also known as an $\epsilon$ that is independent of the specific hypersurface, if and only if the intrinsic Gaussian curvature, denoted as $K$, of M is also greater than zero across the entire hypersurface, denoted as $M$.

A new wireless system concept called multi-service interference suppression (MSIS) is introduced in this paper, which optimizes power allocation to simultaneously maximize data transmission and power harvesting while minimizing interference to coexisting communication systems. An inefficient existing method of power distribution is also examined and criticized for suboptimal data transmission rates and excessive interference. Two innovative methods of power distribution are proposed to address these issues, allowing the SWIPT base station to either minimize interference to a specific communication cell or a aggregate of interfering cells. By formulating an integer linear programming model, the first method results in a solution that maximizes data transmission rates, whereas the second method leads to a convex optimization model that balances power distribution among multiple interfering cells. Furthermore, the paper examines the impact of power distribution on power harvesting and power savings.

The research by Doi and Hara attempts to expand the findings of Cayley's 1878 work, which calculated the number of isomorphism classes of connected graphs with three or more edges, by determining the number of isomorphism classes of connected graphs G whose maximum vertex degree is less than or equal to 4. Specifically, they calculated this number for values of n ranging from 10 to 100 in increments of 10 by utilizing a parallel implementation of Sage, showing that the majority of these graphs have a maximum vertex degree of 4.

The detection sensitivity of seismically isolated test masses in gravitational wave detectors experiences a decrease at frequencies above a few hundred Hertz due to linked residual motion between the test masses and the beam suspension. To enhance the responsiveness of these instruments at high frequencies, a new design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer has been developed by splitting the optical field into two distinct paths, each containing a Michelson Sagnac interferometer with distinct mass drivers and optically coupling the two paths. A frequency response pattern emerges through control of the splitting ratio and phase relationship between the two interferometers, effectively broadening the bandwidth without compromising strain sensitivity or increasing back-action noise. Compared to a standard Michelson interferometer, the benefits of this design are evident, and it provides a 3.5-fold improvement in displacement noise at a specific frequency, making it particularly advantageous for upcoming high-precision gravitational wave detectors like Einstein Telescope.

This research focuses on an extreme scenario in wireless communication where multiple users transmit simultaneously to their respective orthogonal access points in a multi-carrier system, without any interference between their transmission areas. We analyze this unusual scenario where transmission areas are disjoint using a stochastic protocol to determine transmission opportunities. Our study reveals that, under certain conditions, the distribution of the distances from users to their access points matches the distribution of the areas they occupy. Furthermore, this research reveals that in this extreme case, the successful transmission areas conform to a two-step process where larger areas occur at an exponential rate and smaller areas occur at a power law rate, with this process varying based on the transmission probability and transmission loss exponent. Our findings also indicate that the average usable area is significantly higher than previous estimates, potentially providing a substantial improvement in system performance.

Previous studies using high-resolution submillimeter and millimeter continuum imaging have revealed that a significant portion of young stellar systems contain submillimeter-sized structures within their disks, particularly in systems with a mass accretion rate higher than $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ per year. To understand the physical processes occurring around these young stellar systems, it's essential to develop a comprehensive image of their surroundings. While some existing theories propose that these structures result from magnetic instability, they lack consideration for the impact of vertical shear instability (VSI) on the distribution of solid material. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating how VSI affects the formation of submillimeter structures in gas and dust, especially in a scenario where both VSI and magnetic instability are present, as modeled through three-dimensional simulations. It is found that both form of instability can coexist without VSI preventing the formation of submillimeter structures in the model. As a result, our study predicts that regions that experience VSI will exhibit enhanced millimeter emission compared to those that do not, with this feature potentially observable through current imaging capabilities. Moreover, this study also forecasts that the location of VSI will typically be located at a greater distance from the young star than the region that is influenced by magnetic instability, as evidenced by comparisons of simulation models with current imaging data.

A novel axial vector diquark interaction has been incorporated into the Relativistic Quark Model to enhance its predictive capabilities, allowing it to accurately describe the axial vector meson spectrum up to 4 Glueballs and 4 Mesons.  This approach successfully calculates both the mass and the axial vector form factor for each of the 8 mesons, even though there is limited experimental data on form factors at high momentum transfer.  By quark-meson coupling, a range of finite objects including nuclei and gluons found in astronomical objects are calculated.  This model predicts the baryon form factors, nuclear binding energies, the equation of state relevant for neutron stars and white dwarfs, as well as the radii of these objects.  Additionally, it calculates the radiative decay of mesons and the sensitivity of form factors to the mass of the quarks.

This research investigates the robustness of Molmer-Sorensen gates against various frequencies of ion motion in a trapped ion system, showing that equal energy distribution across multiple motion states can significantly reduce gate operations' sensitivity to frequency shifts by up to two orders of magnitude compared to the conventional single-state approach.

Our analysis of Dirac semimetals reveals that including electron-phonon interactions leads to a gap opening at the Fermi surface, with a size determined by the strength of the interaction. A high-sensitivity to crystal structure and parabolic band masses, the interaction can also overcome screening and results in a strong electron-phonon coupling, ultimately causing a Peierls instability and a superconducting transition in a subset of dsymmetries. Support by low linear dispersion masses, interaction-induced gaps in CdSi_2 and CaSi_2 are demonstrated, with predicted values of 100 meV and 20 meV, respectively, and a non-conventional linearly dependent $\Delta(T)$ behavior, exhibiting $T_c$'s of 1.2 K and 0.25 K for these materials.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has the capability to detect new neutral lepton generations at a level that could be significantly higher than current thresholds. The current limits on the neutral lepton's nature were set by the NA48 experiment and recently surpassed by the NA62 experiment in the process $K_{L} \to \pi^{0} e N$. The new limit was set at a level of $10^{-4}$, with a factor of 25 improvement possible. The best theoretical models predict levels of $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$, which are within the range that the NA62 experiment can detect. The proposed analysis strategy will reach these levels, making the NA62 experiment a top-tier benchmark for understanding the properties of a newly discovered neutral lepton, potentially opening up a rich area of physics.

We investigate the use of neural language models for generating text. Our hypothesis is that specifying a an $N$-gram language model as our target allows for efficient learning by a neural model, given the incorporation of a residual learning framework. We find that this approach yields superior results when compared to standard neural models and approaches achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of text quality. Our analysis of the internal mechanisms reveals that neural models adhere to the specified $N$-gram language model, leading to a significant reduction in the clarification task for the model. Our research also shows that this approach can be effectively applied to more complex tasks, including conditional text generation.

Reconstructing 3D faces from unstructured videos poses significant difficulties due to occlusions, variability, and lack of synchronized 3D face data and videos. This project presents a unified framework called SADRNet, which produces aligned input features from videos and employs separate networks to handle face reconstruction and landmark prediction. The structure of SADRNet is inspired by the self-supervised learning technique of contrastive prediction, which dissects the models into separate networks in analogy to contrasting positive and negative samples. By forgoing paired 3D face data and videos, SADRNet thrives on novel methods for handling such data's significant variability. By integrating a landmark branch that processes the same videos and faces as the reconstruction branch, it is possible to exploit the weakly supervised learning capability of mutual feature normalization to efficiently pretrain the network. The result is a framework that excels at predicting subtle facial details from unstructured videos and bypasses the need for synchronized 3D face data and videos. Experiments conducted on the videos of the YouTube Faces dataset and the 3D face data of the MFRA database confirm the efficacy of SADRNet with substantial improvements in performance.

In our study, we investigate the nature of perturbations generated during $\alpha$-attractor inflation, focusing on the parameter regions that lead to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Initially, we investigate the impact of a non-standard vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the inflaton on PBH production. Moreover, we analyze the side-bands resulting from oscillations in the power spectrum. The constraints imposed by the stochastic gravitational wave background and the collapse of PBHs on supermassive black holes are taken into consideration. The outcomes of our investigation are further explored in the context of the dark matter problem and the solution to the matter power spectrum puzzle.

For any labeled ordered tree with n+1 distinct positive integer labels, we can identify a special label known as the deepest vertex. This label corresponds to the node that is furthest from the root when considering the absolute differences between adjacent label values. Our research reveals a fundamental property indicating that the set of all n-element subsets of positive integers, excluding those corresponding to trees, can be characterized by the absence of a deepest vertex in the associated tree with n+1 numbers. Moreover, we establish the count of such valid (n+1)-element sets that satisfy this condition is equal to 2 * A000111(n-1) * A000111(n) / n!.

This investigation utilizes iOCR, an image recognition framework, to obtain
and verify data from election tabulation systems in real-time, with the
aim of enhancing transparency and trust in the process. By directly
interacting with these systems, it serves as a humble attempt to demonstrate
the potential limitations and challenges of current IR technologies in processing
election results. The project encompasses implementing and applying iOCR
to four distinct systems commonly used in municipal elections in the United States.
The outcomes are presented through a suite of tests simulating real counting
scenarios, as well as an actual application during the 2019 local elections in
Montpellier, France. The outcome codes from these elections are available to
the public on GitHub at the following link: this GitHub linkThe abstract for the paper that describes the iTR system, an integrated tool for recognizing and validating image-based tables, has been presented.

In a time series model using an autoregressive approach, an unexpected phenomenon known as benign misfitting occurs when data is generated from a non-stationary model but analyzed with a stationary framework, with the estimated model parameters converging to zero as the sample size increases. This paper investigates the underlying mechanism of benign misfitting in an over-parameterized setting by examining the behavior of intermediate quantities, revealing the interplay between the non-central limit of the least-squares estimator and a random matrix formed by the sum of independent random matrices. The derived insights provide a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges in fitting linear time series models and can lead to improved strategy for model selection.

This research focuses on a distributed version of the storage investment problem where multiple agents collaborate to meet future energy needs. The goal of each individual agent is to maximize their own benefit, considering the potential value of holding storage for future gains. To effectively model this interaction, we developed a game-theoretic approach where the scope of planning and information sharing among the agents can be dynamically adjusted based on risk tolerance and anticipated costs of communication. The results show that more aggressive planning and information sharing lead to outcomes that better meet the system's requirements but also lead to increased communication expenses. The proposed method is evaluated using both simulated data and real-world data from the California energy market, demonstrating its ability to ensure sufficient meeting of demands while minimizing storage costs. The findings highlight the importance of balancing risk tolerance, communication costs, and system efficiency in a range of cooperative storage applications.

A simplified radiative equilibrium model of planetary atmospheres is used to employ a basic circulation pattern comparison across various worlds. This model is suited for atmospheres with thin layers relative to their radius that exhibit rapid rotation in comparison to their thermal equator width. In this context, several models are applicable in comparison. This radiative equilibrium model yields a comparison of circulation patterns that occur around various worlds including Jupiter, Venus, and Mars as well as exoplanets such as hot Jupiters and super-Earths. A general categorization scheme is proposed for these comparison models. This scheme relies on two primary parameters, the ratio of Coriolis force to centrifugal force and the ratio of radiative to turbulent forces. This framework is applied to various worlds including hot Jupites, the atmospheres of Jupiter and Venus, and the early atmosphere of Mars, as well as hypothetical atmospheres for an old Mars and a tropical Venus. This analysis also examines the occurrence of weathering and convection in the early Mars atmosphere and the wave-induced circulation in the old Mars atmosphere in addition to the super-rotation caused by rayleigh number convection in the Venus atmosphere. This model fails to accurately represent the complex circulation patterns observed in the current Mars and Venus atmospheres. It also fails to accurately represent the heat redistribution occurring in the dayside of hot Jupiter atmospheres.

Deep learning models trained on large datasets generally exhibit strong performance when deployed independently, however their effectiveness can be compromised in dynamic environments where underlying data distributions change over time. This paper investigates the dynamic learning process for a neural network, specifically in the context of a high-dimensional classifier with limited labeled training data. We provide an analytical approach using Reinforcement Learning (RL) to determine the optimal neural update rule when data distributions undergo sudden or gradual changes. Our method is designed to be computationally efficient, as it does not rely on expensive numerical optimizations. Experimental results demonstrate that our neural learning framework successfully adapts to both abrupt and gradual shifts in data, outperforming existing methods when there are significant changes. Notably, our analysis and corresponding neural update policy are applicable to high-throughput, large-scale machine learning scenarios.

Researchers have utilized a sophisticated theoretical approach called multi-valley effective weight theory (MVEWT) to accurately model the electronic and structural properties of a specific defect in silicon known as (AlIn)_Si. This defect has multiple interchangeable configuration forms that impact its electrical characteristics and have significant implications for controlling the behavior of silicon-based technology at the atomic level. By employing CI-STO code derived from MVEWT, the exact properties of three (AlIn)_Si defect configurations were studied in detail, taking into account the nuances of five s-band electrons, relativistic effects, and the complexities of crystal lattice distortions. These simulations have enabled the development of reliable models to predict how (AlIn)_Si configurations behave in response to the application of external electrical fields and temperature changes, as well as providing precise values for predicting the outcomes of experimental techniques such as deep level transient spectroscopy and magnetic resonance imaging.

Our theoretical model examines the transport properties of a particular quantum structure known as a semiconductor trench with a hexagonal lattice and is located within a strong perpendicular magnetic field. We specifically analyze a hgte-based trench that lies just below its critical thickness where it exhibits strong spin-orbit effects. By simulating its energy spectrum, we observe the formation of distinct, highly localized Caroli-Matveev-Lashkevich-Shvartsman states around each atomic site in the transverse direction. When we introduce electrodes and calculate current-voltage characteristics, we observe asymmetric current flow due to the absence of a energy gap, and there is evidence of non-reciprocity under a reversed magnetic field configuration. Furthermore, we detect hfsb-like backscognition in reversed bias conditions and find that it and nonreciprocity disappear when the trench becomes a quantum dot at a critical thickness. Ultimately, such TQS structures are considered promising candidates for the precise observation of subtle quantum phenomena and the development of robust, scalable spintronic and mesoscopic quantum devices.

In this paper, a novel Mixed Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) model is introduced to enhance the efficiency of 5G networks by dynamically allocating uplink and downlink subchannels based on traffic demands while minimizing interference between neighboring cells. A game-theoretic approach is taken to select optimal TDD models for base stations in a heterogeneous network, considering the significant energy savings associated with turning off unused radios. The non-cooperative model proposed leads to a dominant strategy equilibrium, allowing BSc to allocate models independently and achieve maximum system throughput. Furthermore, energy consumption is considered in an enhanced cooperative model, where a penalty is imposed on differing models to minimize the number of active radios. The proposed model considers three TDD modes: full uplink, full downlink, and a combined model. Theoretical proofs and numerical examples validate the proposed model's effectiveness.

Recent advancements in neural ODE/ODE networks have relied on traditional gradient-based training methods, which presuppose the availability of a graph structure for the network and its Hamiltonian to facilitate the calculation of gradients. Nevertheless, we introduce a novel framework that enables the acquisition of gradients in neural ODE/ODE networks without a graph structure, by training the network's and its Hamiltonian's parameters through a Hamiltonian neural network. We validate our approach through diverse numerical experiments.

A lone expert is able to review and give a reliability rating for an agent's decisions, which are then used to identify and fix any errors. This human-in-the-loop approach results in a more trustworthy and accurate model than simply training on more data human alone can provide.

We define a novel quantum invariant, denoted as $\tau_q$, for 2-chains within the interval bundle of a torus, $T^2 \times I$. This invariant satisfies a set of intrinsic criteria and involves the application of the q-Kostant polynomial during its calculation. By deriving a second, independent invariant, $\tilde{\tau}_q$, we establish an analogy between the classical and quantum cases, much like the relationship initially discovered by Novik and Skalski. The inequality $\log |\tau(a)\tau(b)\tau(c)| \leq \delta$ mirrors the condition found in the study of flat bundles by Nikolov and Segal, where $\delta$ is a value directly related to the area of a specific geometric figure known as Dehn's polygon. The properties of this invariant also enable us to determine the conjugacy classes of pairs of elements that define representations which constitute points in the set described by the condition above.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with a variety of strategies being developed to further enhance performance.  The context of BERT is constructed from sub-words, which inherently limits the context available for each instance, thus restricting the potential for learning dependent relations crucial for WSD.  In contrast, dictionary entries, with their comprehensive definitions, provide a rich source of information that can be used to enhance the context for BERT-based WSD.  By incorporating both dictionary entries and target words, a rigorous set of data can be created, enabling BERT to effectively learn dependent relations and thereby improve performance on WSD.  A novel approach known as context-gloss enhancement is proposed, which ranks the senses of a word based on BERT's classification of enhanced contexts.  The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing previous context-enhancement strategies by a significant margin.

This study formulates a genuine integral definition of the reciprocal Gamma function, overcoming the limitations of the standard contour-based definitions. It is demonstrated that a uniquely specified, non-emptiness regularized version of the set of all possible integral definitions of the reciprocal Gamma function can be achieved, resulting in a novel expression: $\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)}=\exp\left(\,1+\gamma+\,z\,\log(z)+\,\displaystyle\,\int_{0}^{\infty}\,\frac{\,\log\left(\,1-\,\exp\left(-\,t\,\right)\,\right)-\,\exp\left(-\,t\,\right)-\,\frac{\,\left(\,\log\left(\,t\,\right)+\gamma\,\right)\,\left(\,\exp\left(-\,t\,\right)-\,\exp\left(-\,z\,t\,\right)\,\right)}{\,\,1-\,\exp\left(-\,t\,\right)\,\,}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\

Using large color complexes created in p-A collisions, this research aims to confirm the presence of top quark production. By confirming top quark production, it paves the way for utilizing PGCs to prove their lack of suppression in these collisions. To identify top quark production, careful analysis of specific decay signals is required to distinguish it from similar processes like bottom quark pair production. If top quark production is confirmed, it enables the prediction of light quark suppression in PGC-induced collisions.

The texts and structured queries in diverse domains are parsed into structured representations for database questioning, yet current cross-domain text-to-SQL models suffer from low generalizability due to the lack of diverse, structured representation across supported databases. To address this, we introduce a cross-domain SQL parsing framework supported by multiple tiny databases, enabling the questions to be uniquely represented and facilitate learning for cross-domain SQL parsing. Our framework employs a list representation that encodes the supported databases to question, a content-aware mean representation that uses the most likely table in the list, and a multi-task learning approach with a single-table SQL parsing as a supportive task. Our method is evaluated on a synthetic multi-domain SQL parsing dataset, showing consistent improvements in accuracy and the quality of parsed representations.

This paper investigates differential privacy within the framework of graphs for computing confidential aggregate metrics. We break down the applicable graphs into three main categories: knowledge graphs, social networks, and communication graphs, and discuss privacy threats in each category. We then explore how an DP mechanism can be implemented to protect different types of graphs while adhering to the composition properties of DP. However, existing DP formulations for various graph-organized data fail to combine in the same way due to their distinct threat models. We analyze the compositional properties of DP in the context of three categories of graphs and propose novel formulations of DP that facilitate combination and comparison of prior formulations. We also compare and contrast the DP mechanisms for different categories of graphs in order to highlight the challenges of achieving combination. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for the design of confidential graph-based computation systems that incorporate multiple sources of data organized as graphs.

The vast amount of data anticipated from the Euclid survey, with its expected
record size exceeding 1 zettabyte even after compression, is expected to
encourage the continued development and deployment of cutting-edge techniques for
image processing, analysis, and management. These developments are projected to
have significant benefits for the communities utilizing the Euclid data, as well
as other communities working with large-scale weak lensing and galaxy survey data
sets, effectively creating a pathway for Euclid to build upon the legacy of
predecessor projects such as DES, KiDS, and HSC. In this presentation, we will
examine various weak lensing collaboration software developments in depth,
categorizing them into three generations and outlining the characteristics that
define each generation, while also highlighting the scientific achievements
realized by each collaboration generation. Furthermore, we will outline the
characteristics and scientific achievements that are likely to be realized by
future generations, effectively projecting the Euclid legacy in terms of analysis
techniques that it is likely to contribute to and employ.

A new stochastic approach is presented to derive macroscopic equations from the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, termed the random hydrodynamics (RHD) method, and its extension, the phase-space random hydrodynamics (PSRHD) method, which incorporates the Weyl symbol approximation. These methods yield identical results when applying the normal ordering approximation. Both RHD and PSRHD approaches include quantum pressure and are applicable to both equilibrium and non-equilibrium scenarios for interacting Bose fluids. When using a contact interaction, the PSRHD method produces a modified Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GP) equation, distinct from the GP equation in a mean-field approximation. This new PSRHD equation is also described by a unique modified Lagrangian.

We've developed extensive deviation principles for independent and identically distributed letters from an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$, applying to the word $w_n$ composed of the most recent $n$ letters that share $n$ common adjacent letters. These letters are randomly selected from the alphabet based on a specified distribution of the single-letter words made from the most recent $n$ letters. We've established that if the probability of $w_n$ exceeds $\rho_n$, then the expected number of words up to length $n$ with the same structure as $w_n$ is at most $\rho_n^{-1} n + C$ for some constant $C$. If the probability of $w_n$ is at most $\rho_n$, we've found an lower bound for the maximum expected number of distinct adjacent letter pairs that can be formed up to length $n$. These principles generalize and build upon the work of Gou\"e and Merkle (2022).

We introduce the concept of a region-minimizing surface within a metric space's homotopy class, specifically on the boundary of certain spaces. It is demonstrated that in a Minkowski spacetime's causal structure, there exists a causally minimizing surface within a specific homotopy class on the boundary. Furthermore, the criteria for a Minkowski spacetime's causal future past boundary to possess a particular geometric property are established, which in turn guarantees the existence of a causally minimizing surface within any of its homotopy classes. This condition is also related to a specific geometric characteristic of the spacetime, denoted as being $c$-marginally trapping.

Recent absolute minimum in the isovector monopole tensor interaction channel has been identified at a very low spin, specifically $0^{-}$, in Nickel-64. Our study places the tensor interaction at the center of a theoretical analysis. By examining three nickel isotopes - Nickel-60, Nickel-62, and Nickel-64 - we investigate the coexistence of two atomic states at the same energy level. These states are characterized by a negative and a positive parity, respectively, and their interaction leads to energy level splitting. By analyzing electric quadrupole transitions between high-j nucleonic orbitals and utilizing a theoretical model that incorporates the interplay of the shell model and collective rotation, we predict transition probabilities that can be experimentally verified. Our calculations accurately match existing data on transition energies and electric quadrupole moments, but unfortunately, there are limited data on electric quadrupole transitions for all three isotopes. The tensor interaction is shown to be the primary factor in determining the energy level splitting pattern. In particular, we calculate a splitting of 22 keV, 31 keV, and 43 keV for Nickel-60, Nickel-62, and Nickel-64, respectively. The predicted splitting for Nickel-64 falls within the reachable energy range for future experiments at the FAIR facility.
