This paper introduces the J-K fold cross-validation technique, an innovative approach designed to reduce the variance commonly encountered during the tuning of machine learning model hyperparameters in natural language processing. Additionally, we introduce the JC-virtual technique, which leverages additional training data generated by shuffling labels to create supplementary validation sets. Our method involves ranking validation folds based on performance and selecting the corresponding subsets for training and testing. We evaluate the J-K fold and JC-virtual techniques across multiple tasks including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and question answering, achieving comparable results to conventional dropout-based validation while significantly enhancing stability and reducing computational costs. Our findings indicate that this technique enhances model performance by approximately 2% on average, with a substantial improvement of 5% to 10% observed in certain cases.

This paper discusses an approach called Instructor-Pupil Framework (IPF) in the context of knowledge acquisition. This framework involves two main components, an instructor who possesses partial knowledge and a pupil with no knowledge, interacting to build upon the initial information provided. The IPF approach has various applications in knowledge acquisition, including creating expert systems, enhancing classification performance, and gaining control over neural networks. The section on application discussions in this paper specifically focuses on knowledge acquisition through the IPF method and its relevance to neural networks.

The probability energy function commonly employed as a guide for modeling Markov random fields represents the negative log of the marginal probability in a specific configuration. Although this energy function enables efficient inference through methods like Metropolis-Hastings, calculating it can be computationally intensive in graphical models. We develop an efficient method to calculate the probability energy function on a triangle-factorizable graph by leveraging the existing structure and relationships within the graph and its dual. This approach allows us to not only compute the probability energy function but also to perform exact minimum potential energy estimation and the optimization of a given configuration with significantly reduced computational demand. In comparison to traditional methods, our algorithm provides a significant improvement in efficiency, offering a 5-fold to 20-fold reduction in computational requirements for MPE estimation and optimization tasks.

We analyzed the photon recoil effects in single-beam absorption spectroscopy used to characterize small vapor concentrations of strontium. By simulating absorption spectra, we determined that photon recoil significantly broadens the expected width of the spectra, particularly in single-beam experiments. This effect manifests as a shift in frequency of about 1 kHz and was observed in our data. We also found that photon recoil causes the transit width to increase by approximately 10% with a 10 cm beam width. These results are applicable to a range of applications in addition to absorption spectroscopy, including saturation height measurements, EM field detection, and time-domain ring-down experiments.

When a shear-aligned polymer solution flows through a narrow channel, there are
several scenarios in which the polymers shift from following the flow to forming
head-tail orientations perpendicular to the flow direction. We analyzed transition
points for shear alignment and band splitting transitions in multiple types of
narrow channels to see if different channel shapes require different physical
mechanisms to explain the observed shifts. By compiling transition data from
several experiments with different channel shapes, we found a unified scaling
relationship that accurately reflects the location of the transition points
across all geometries. This suggests that a single physical mechanism, likely
involving the balance of flow and wall effects near a channel's closure, governs
these transitions regardless of the specific geometry.

This paper aims to explain and extend the concepts of Racah algebras, originating in the context of Lie algebra representation theory. We explore their applications to $n$-point closure algebras, specifically focusing on $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. We present $n$ generators for this algebra and its quotient, the Pachner algebra, both of which are associated with the $(2,2,n)$-Pachner polygon. Notably, we provide a generalization of a sequence first identified by Helton and Rostecki, which we call the Hilbert-Poincaré sequence of the Pachner algebra, as well as for $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. We also discuss relevant literature on the topics of Racah algebras, their applications, and the related Lie algebra U(n) within the context of the Schrödinger algebra U(d).

All Web-based services provided by Google are personalized to a user's specific
needs, an advantage that's been widely accepted.  The degree to which Google
customization influences all aspects of knowledge discovery has been an open
question that's been heavily debated within the research community.  In this study,
we use careful observation and careful measurement to determine the degree to which
Google's search engine influences neutral, factual content found on web pages.
The data collected from five carefully selected web pages over five days' time
shows that Google's search engine is capable of influencing what parts of text are
visible to a user's naked eye over time.  In contrast, five carefully selected
pages that are devoid of any kind of user-specific data remained consistently
unchanged during the same period of study.  The implications of this period of study
are discussed in this study.

A next-generation accelerator facility is proposed, capable of colliding 1 TeV protons with 800 GeV muons. The potential discoveries in this setting could encompass the Higgs boson and a wide range of weakly interacting particles. These capabilities significantly exceed those achievable in electron-proton collisions at the same energy level. Drawing from extensive analyses of the E143, HERMES, and RHIC experiments as well as the HERA and RHIC accelerator facilities, this proposed muon-ion collider could offer comprehensive insights into QED and QCD interactions.

We present a novel MRI sequence, based on a modified turbo spin-echo technique, 
that produces free-breathing 4D (three-dimensional image space plus time) T2-weighted MRI scans 
of the entire body or body parts. This method produces consistent, high-contrast, T2-weighted 
images of the body, regardless of the patient's breathing pattern. It has been tested in 
one-dimensional and two-dimensional image acquisitions, and demonstrates its effectiveness 
and robustness in one hundred and seven free-breathing one-dimensional, five-dimensional, 
and two-dimensional (three-dimensional image space plus time) MRI scans of the body. It 
also compares favorably to breath-held MRI scans in terms of high-contrast, T2-weighted 
images of the body, despite being slightly thinner in thickness. It has since been 
used in one hundred and seven free-breathing one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional 
MRI scans of the body, and shows its effectiveness in producing high-contrast, T2-weighted 
images of the body, plus additional breath-signals for verification during respiratory
navigation or further analysis.

Automatic testing of software metrics has traditionally relied on synthetic data, 
which fails to accurately represent real-world data due to its inadequate 
representation. This paper introduces a Paired-Permutation Test (PPT) specifically 
tailored for structured metrics, overcoming previous limitations of PPT in this 
context. The proposed method enables the examination of the significance of 
metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, halting probability, and semantic 
similarity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of PPT to non-deterministic
tree-based metrics including approximate data-flow graphs (aDAG) and their 
similarity measure aDAG-Rank. The results reveal that various metrics genuinely 
contribute to the predictability of bug presence in software, yet there's also 
evidence of spurious correlations in tree-based metrics and lower complexity 
requirements for PPT comparisons of metric trees.

This comprehensive dataset combines yearly freight shipping statistics for U.S. cargo vessels spanning the period from 1966 to 2016, filling a gap in existing data that excluded 1966 data provided by Cox (2018). The primary source for the data is the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (1971-, 1972, and 1973), with supplementary information drawn from Cox (2018) and U.S. Department of Commerce (1967 to 1970). The integrated dataset opens up new research possibilities by allowing direct comparisons and analyses between past and present periods, specifically with access to 1966 data.

A new class of distance metrics, specifically F$_{v}$, is introduced for probability distributions, extending the concept of fabric distances initially proposed by Kallabis and Panaretsos. F$_{v}$ distances are related to both f-divergences and the Hellinger distance, and for a specific choice of function, it provides an upper limit for the Hellinger distance. A connection is also established between F$_{v}$ and the Tsallis divergence, indicating that for values of $v$ between 0 and 2, F$_{v}$ is proportional to the Tsallis divergence with a corresponding constant. Visualizing F$_{v}$ distances for various functions and values of $v$ through Sankey diagrams and 3D surfaces, and performing a 3D wireframe visualization of the 'hellering cat' by scaling a 2D $\rho$-plot against axes defined by two T-divergences.

The recent interest in using large language models for forecasting numerical indicators has been driven by the success of BERT, which was previously primarily used for different tasks. The research team members employed the Spacy and Transformers libraries to process and integrate data for a stock prediction model based on BERT, resulting in the creation of a compact JSON format that included information about the stock's previous and current state, as well as its future value. The original dataset from 2006 to the present was used for training and testing the model, and the Month-on-Month change in stock prices was implemented as the $Y$ variable to increase the model's accuracy. To accelerate the model's training process and reduce the computational costs associated with GPU rental, various techniques such as dropout, data shuffling, and gradient accumulation were applied. The trained BERT model was then combined with a Generative Adversarial Network to generate additional training data, allowing for a month-by-month prediction format for the stock prices.

We investigated double Higgs production at TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders to probe the nature of the Higgs boson. The process was modeled beyond the Standard Theory using two Effective Field Theory frameworks. The first is the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, and the second is an extension of the Two-Step Higgs mechanism where new heavy particles influence both tree-level and higher-order processes in double Higgs production. The relative significance and expected number of signal events were calculated for various International Linear Collider parameters and heavy particle masses. The analysis indicates that with $\sqrt{s}=1.36$ TeV and $\sqrt{s}=1.5$ TeV, the collector can anticipate $\mathcal{O}(10)$ events for a 500 GeV charm superpartner, whereas for a 1 TeV top superpartner, the expectation is near zero even with 500 hours of operation. These predictions assume a specific cutoff in the effective field theories, but the analysis remains robust against changes in this assumption.

We begin by examining the fundamental stresses and forces in a given region of space for a classical particle system, which leads us to define these concepts in terms of a stress-force Lagrangian. Subsequently, we adapt this framework to classical gravity, exploring both the particulate and continuous scenarios. For the latter, we consider it in its linearized and fully nonlinear forms, whether consisting of a scalar, a vector, or a tensor field, in a given spacetime adhering to Newton's laws or Einstein's theory of general relativity.

This study investigates the drag asymmetry experienced by a cylindrical solid as it moves through a granular bed filled with fluid, both where the fluid flows freely and where it experiences fluid resistance. The aspect ratio of the cylinder, defined by its length to diameter, in the free-flow free regime shows a degree of asymmetry in drag experienced in the forward and backward direction for all aspect ratios tested, in line with previous studies, though this behavior shows no dependence on the aspect ratio, in contrast to the drag behavior in the regime of fluid resistance where the aspect ratio does influence the difference in drag experienced in the forward and backward direction. This study also delves on the flow patterns created by the cylinder as it moves through the free-flow free and fluid resistance regimes, both for cylinders with small and large aspect ratios, revealing that the number of vortexes in the cylinder's wake, both behind and in front of the cylinder, is directly related to the aspect ratio.

Our research utilizes an event generator based on the multiphase transport model to analyze the initial anisotropic fluctuations in three dimensions from various heavy ion collisions, specifically looking at the relationship between the second anisotropic flow and the transverse particle momentum. By plotting $p_T$ against effective momentum, we create correlation diagrams to analyze these relationships and then compare them with experimental data from the STAR collaboration. Our results show a clear connection between initial anisotropic fluctuations and triangular flow in two dimensions, but the relationship is less apparent in three dimensions due to other influencing factors such as flow freeze-out conditions and flow conservation effects. Our findings suggest that initial anisotropic fluctuations should not be considered in isolation when analyzing $v_3$ in experimental settings.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is well-suited for searching for violations of time-reversal symmetry in particle physics and for measuring the frequencies of rare particle decays. This paper reviews results achieved in these areas using data from multilepton and multiple photon events, specifically in $B$-meson decays. In terms of violations of time-reversal symmetry, research focuses on interferometric phases derived from $B^0\bar{B^0}$ and $B^+B^+$ decays, originally predicted by the Standard Model and later explored experimentally by the LHCb collaboration. Moreover, this research presents initial measurements of rare decay processes including $B$-meson flavor-changing neutral currents with signatures involving multileptons or photons, for which theoretical predictions suggest very low probabilities, in the range of $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-5}$ per decay.

We develop and evaluate preconditioners tailored for the common approach of combining high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods with implicit time-stepping solvers, typically Krylov subspace methods like GMRES. Given the large scale of resulting systems and their complex, jacobian-like structure, we focus on efficient and scalable solutions by constructing block-based preconditioners. These preconditioners utilize inverse elements from the system matrix and its diagonal, with an attempt to preserve the original system's shapes, including maxwell solvers. In cases where the original system's inverse is not available, we develop and apply suitable alternatives. Through extensive testing using model problems, we compare various combinations of solvers, preconditioners, and time-integrators, showcasing the effectiveness of our methods.

Radiation therapy treatment verification poses significant challenges due to the potential for subtle, three-dimensional tissue deformations that may indicate the presence of tumors or other abnormalities present within the abdomen. Traditional imaging methods used for detection purposes often involve high levels of radiation, CT being a prime example, whereas ultrasound imaging uses sound waves for imaging but can be affected by surrounding gas pockets and produces varying images from one examination to the next due to their two-dimensional nature. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, researchers are now exploring the development of a novel verification method capable of identifying deformations by aligning pre-treatment volume images with post-treatment surface images. In order to achieve this alignment, the proposed approach employs a biomechanical model that can be tailored to the specific characteristics of the tissue in question, filters out unnecessary noise in ultrasound images, and incorporates various constraints to ensure the accuracy of the resulting deformation field, with the primary evaluation of this approach taking place in the context of abdominal verification.

Most self-supervised scene flow estimation models are heavily influenced by the size of their datasets, which lead to a computational bottleneck in the training process. This article proposes a novel approach to mitigate this issue by bypassing the need for pixel-level flow labels and instead focuses on learning the metric properties of flow values in a supervised manner from annotated outlier scenes. Although this method provides a marginal improvement in data-driven settings, it significantly becomes vulnerable to successful attacks when subjected to adversarial video pairs, highlighting the complexity of the task and the limited robustness of current scene flow models. To address this challenge, the paper presents a unified framework for metric learning that integrates the task of flow estimation, leveraging the majority of the model's features for robust metric learning. Experimental results show that this framework achieves superior performance in both metric learning and main task performance when compared to the state-of-the-art results.

Categorizing objects or events based on past experiences is a fundamental capability in biological systems. To achieve this efficiently with limited energy resources, the brain employs a high-firing-rate neural system. In contrast, current artificial neural network approaches generate excessive data and demand substantial energy for processing and storage when dealing with complex tasks involving numerous classes. To address this challenge, we developed a novel algorithm that leverages a Spiking Random Neural Network (RRNN) to perform complex classification tasks in a manner that is both rapid and energy-friendly. This network is capable of self-learning and produces a compact set of features for each class, significantly reducing the amount of data required for further processing. We called this technique the Compressed Class Representation (CCR). Each class is represented by a single spike pattern, which allows the network to perform any subsequent classification using a minimal energy cost. We tested this algorithm on various complex tasks involving image classification and audio classification, and the results show that it significantly improves performance while minimizing energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This research examines the thermodynamic characteristics of a spin-aligned strange quark star under the influence of a strong magnetic field at high temperatures, specifically within the range of 0 to 2 times the critical temperature ($T_c$). Utilizing the improved dense instanton liquid model, we have derived the leading-order and next-to-leading-order equations of motion in the 1/D and 1/$\beta$ expansions to better understand the behavior of this phenomenon. By employing the theorems of dimensional and dimensional reduction, we have obtained the 1D effective potential from which the leading-order and next-to-leading-order equation of state can be determined. In order to solve for our system, we have utilized the Bayesian method to find the self-consistent spin-aligned strange quark star in the presence of a strong magnetic field at various temperatures. Furthermore, we have analyzed the stability of our system by examining the thermodynamic grand canonical potential and canonical potential density. Our findings reveal that the self-consistent strange star can endure a strong magnetic field at any temperature within the range of 0 to 2 times $T_c$. Additionally, we have observed that the impact of the next-to-leading-order correction becomes increasingly significant with the strengthening of the magnetic field at any given temperature.

This research is driven by interesting problems concerning graph pairings, Hamiltonian cycles, and edge coloring. We extend a recent concept of institution pairings by introducing the notion of ideal pairings for graphs with three edges per connected component, demonstrating that such graphs naturally possess an ideal pairing. Furthermore, for cubic graphs, we define a more complex structure called a tinting, consisting of four interconnected parts: a directed graph, a set of undirected edges, a set of 2-cycles, and a set of triple-cycles. We show that any graph with this tinting includes a Hamiltonian cycle, and conversely, that any graph with this property can be tinted in multiple ways. Additionally, we define a more complex structure called a super-tinting, consisting of directed edges, undirected edges, and edge-tuples, and show that such graphs naturally possess a super-tinting and thus a tinting, which also implies the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle.

In highly distributed systems with containerized components, the proliferation of system calls makes debugging and optimization difficult to visualize. To simplify this process, developers would benefit from a call graph that accurately reflects the interdependencies between system calls. However, existing call-graph construction techniques either ignore the properties of individual containers or are computationally prohibitive for large-scale applications. To address this challenge, we introduced Timeloops, an efficient technique that produces tight call graphs by combining the analysis of individual programs. Timeloops starts by constructing a crude graph from the system calls of each program, and then refines this representation by iteratively refining the connections between programs in a data-driven manner. We integrated Timeloops into Bazel, the build system for Google, and evaluated it against the Bazel's millions of dependencies. This assessment demonstrated that Timeloops could be computed in under 30 seconds for Bazel's vast build graph.

This research enhances the Probabilistic Multiple Birth Model (PMBM) filter by developing a new approach to estimate the probability density of newly appearing targets. By reusing existing lattice-based filtering techniques, the proposed method efficiently calculates this probability density within an existing lattice structure, avoiding the computational burden of creating and managing a new, separate lattice. A more diagonal grid structure is recommended to minimize errors and maximize accuracy. The effectiveness of the new approach is demonstrated through various target detection scenarios in the context of sensor management applications.

This study examines the null controllability of a species dynamics model, governed by a hyperbolic equation with a degenerate elliptic internal growth term in a spatial domain. The model's control mechanism operates over a time and space subset of the overall domain. Following the establishment of a Carleman estimate for a related adjoint model, we prove the existence of a localized control function capable of driving the system's state to zero over time. Subsequent to these existence proofs, we explore additional properties of the control function, including those of its norm, in the context of the system's initial conditions.

A reinforcement learning-based method for soccer decision making is examined, focusing on three complex game situations that have been overlooked in previous research. The examined situations revolve around corner kicks, free kicks, and goals scored by one team. Corner kicks and free kicks are highly intricate due to their susceptibility to opposing team interventions, whereas goals scored by one team create an opportunity for either team to take the field. Our analysis compares multiple state and action space representations, as well as different learning strategies, including leveraging game history. The results show that utilizing the recent game's situation and employing a combination of value and policy gradients leads to significant improvements, allowing for more informed in-game decisions by corner kick takers, free kick takers, and teams following scored goals.

Waveform inversion (WSI) is a key technique in seismic imaging that integrates high-resolution images with accurate physics-based modeling to guide full-waveform imaging and catalyst for efficient initial model for tomography. A critical aspect of WSI is the utilization of migration-scattered waves in updating the subsurface properties. Recently, the use of migrated data has been supplemented with expanded source (ES) technology, which in addition to enhancing imaging efficiency, also reduces computational demands in WSI. This paper introduces the concept of ESI in the context of frequency-domain WSI using the Iterative Full-space Source (IFS) method to expand source coverage. The proposed IFS-ES-WSI approach in its current implementation is computationally similar to the standard migrated data WSIs (WSI-PS) in updating subsurface properties, but it offers significant advantages in terms of acceleration and modeling when employing large source arrays. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of IFS-ES-WSI through a series of 2D and a3D time-lapse seismic cases, which in comparison to the standard WSI-PS workflow, showed substantial improvements in imaging results and reduction in computational demands.

To understand the influence of a binary binary colonization process on a larger population set, a randomized voter model with balance conditions was modeled. The model includes site occupation through random diffusion, slow species competition, and elimination of the trailing species, and was analyzed without scale-dependent feedback. The model exhibited a complex species dynamics that resulted in the coexistence of specific species pairs at the elimination phase, and was confirmed through simulations of a non-stochastic version of the model. The coexistence condition was found to be valid for both ideal gas initial distribution and Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics produced during the elimination process, but could be affected by external feedback.

This research report examines the mutual interference between two systems: an intelligent-reflecting surface (IRS)-assisted data transmission system and an IRI-assisted power transmission system, where a device-to-device (D2D) link is being used. The primary objective is to maximize the data transmission system's performance while ensuring that the power transmission system's D2D transmission rate meets a minimum threshold. To effectively manage the computational complexity of this problem, it is divided into two subproblems based on the coupling between the diagonal elements and the structure of the matrix constraint. By applying a block coordinate descent (BCD) approach, the problem is then further simplified into convex optimization subproblems that can be resolved with existing techniques. The proposed solution converges to a stationary point and is demonstrated through simulation results.

To provide laser Doppler velocimetry systems with enhanced safety, remote control capabilities have been developed. The primary objective of this paper is to present the technical aspects of realising such a system in a single-point configuration that outputs two dimensional measurements. The document is structured as follows: the first section presents the key features of a two-point LDV system; the second section describes the adaptation necessary to convert this two-point system to a remote single-point configuration; and the third and final section describes the measures required to enable this system to obtain two dimensional measurements.

The investigation centers on examining the effectiveness of 2-fD programmable phase disks in mitigating spatial aberrations in a TEM system. By applying both theoretical modeling and empirical data, the research reveals that certain configurations of phase disks can significantly reduce the impact of spherical and chromatic aberrations when encountering multi-energy electrons. The study further explores the limitations of phase disks in correcting multi-energy errors and suggests potential strategies to overcome these constraints.

This research examines the spectral and orbital stability of the ground state for the equation that describes the anharmonic oscillator and the Klein-Gordon equation, either in its standard or non-standard forms. It confirms that the standard anharmonic oscillator has a fully stable ground state, and establishes conditions that, if met, also indicate complete stability for the non-standard version.

We derive new outcomes regarding exact quotients in the group of units within certain non-commutative rational numbers using Sanut's theory. These units are defined relative to various orderings within a specific category of quadratic modules, and this derivation relies on a local and global reciprocity law recently established by Enochs and Jansons. The analysis of the derived formulas yields insights into the behavior of the local and global units for these non-commutative rational numbers.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral particles like axion-like particles (ALPs) is typically done by analyzing the decay products visible in the data. However, a different approach involves searching for ALPs based on the missing transverse momentum they create. This paper aims to bridge the gap between these two methods by calculating how ALPs produced from the decay of B-mesons can escape detection, considering all possible sources of missing energy. A comprehensive calculation of this phenomenon is presented, taking into account the effects of hadronization and color reconnection, which can lead to an ALP or a photon being emitted from hadrons rather than from the primary decay. This calculation was then applied to simulate data from Belle II, yielding estimates of the frequency with which ALPs produced from B-meson decays go undetected or appear as missing energy at the Belle II experiment site.

When a star undergoes a supernova explosion, it leaves behind a rapidly spinning neutron star or black hole.  Given a population of these objects, researchers can analyze the behavior of their rotations to gain insights into the fundamental physics they comprise.  However, this approach relies on a crucial assumption: that the objects' rotations align with a specific axis in space.  By investigating a proposed superradiant instability in neutral mesons, researchers found that even misaligned rotations could provide valuable information about the mass of these mesons within a narrow range.  Drawing on observations from the LAMOST survey, researchers studied 24 massive quasars, examining the broad lines produced by winds around them.  By analyzing the relationships between the widths of these lines and the velocities of the quasars, researchers were able to estimate the masses of individual quasars.  After correcting for potential sources of error, researchers found that the expected patterns of the superradiant instability did not match the results obtained from the quasar analyses.  Although there was some disagreement with previous studies, researchers were able to establish an upper limit on the mass of the mesons, concluding that they are likely produced by superradiance in less than one twenty-third of a Planck mass squared.

During the retinal development in vertebrates, the migration of cell nuclei between the retina's base and surface is observed. While previous studies have linked this interkinetic nuclear movement (INM) to the timing of cell division, some evidence points to this movement serving a more purposeful function by transporting the nucleus and associated genetic material closer to the site of differentiation in the retina. However, to date, this hypothesis has lacked experimental confirmation. Our research, focused on the zebrafish model, proposes that the INM serves a dispersive function, facilitating the even distribution of neurogenic commitment within the retinal layer. This finding is supported by the discovery that cells determined to differentiate externally express the transcription factor Prdm1 at their level of intensity, prdm1 absence resulting in the accumulation of these expressions near the retina's base. The retinal development beyond the INM stage relies on the expression of Prdm1, as its absence leads to a lack of INM and an inadequate expansion of the retina. This study highlights the role of the INM as essential not only for timing cell division but also for promoting the even distribution of cells committed to differentiate and thereby enhancing their overall efficiency.

In the processes of color image demosaicing and video compressive sensing, it is crucial to accurately identify the borders of objects or sources to minimize errors and improve the quality of the output. However, existing algorithms typically fail to produce precise source boundaries due to their reliance on inaccurate or computationally expensive methods. Existing solutions also struggle to effectively integrate the results of edge detection models into subsequent reconstruction steps. In response, we have developed two integrative algorithms that leverage the outputs of a state-of-the-art edge detection model, specifically the Coarse-to-Fine Network (CFNet), as prior knowledge in order to segment sources and incorporate their results into the compressive sensing process. The first algorithm, designed for color image demosaicing, employs a Fourier Transform-based optimization method and achieves superior results compared to existing algorithms on widely-used test datasets. The second algorithm, tailored for compressive video sensing, utilizes a sparse representation to achieve significant improvements in PSNR and structural similarity metrics across multiple test cases. Both algorithms take the predictions of the CFNet as side information in order to produce more accurate source boundaries and incorporate their results into the reconstruction process through iterative optimization procedures, specifically the Coherent Gradient Descent (CGD) and the Coherent Descent (CD) algorithms.

This research extends the development of polar active fluid models in the context of inertialess dynamics, where the particle interactions follow a power-law with an exponent $\alpha$. Unlike previous studies that assumed random and directionally symmetric two-body interactions, we explore the effects of unique two-body interactions unique to each component of the fluid. These interactions can be attractive or repulsive and cannot change across the fluid. As a result, they create a wide array of motifs that significantly influence the structure and scattering patterns of the fluid, especially when considering different dimensions and angles. These patterns mirror those observed in solutions to Lorentz gases but with distinct characteristics due to the three-body nature of the scattering process. Ultimately, this study provides valuable insights into the complex dynamics of polar active fluids and the impact of irreversible disorder on their behavior.

Existing research on document extraction typically focuses on specific elements such as text, images, or metadata. In contrast, this work integrates natural language processing into the extraction framework, resulting in structured JSON output that includes all essential components required to utilize the information contained within the document.

Researchers have applied the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to solve the quantum harmonic oscillator system given an initial displaced state and a time-varying frequency, obtaining the full wavefunction through discrete time steps. The expectation values of the position and momentum operators were then calculated.

The YORP effect is a phenomenon where solar radiation pressure causes a change in an asteroid's rotation as it resists the torque generated by absorbed and scattered sunlight and thermal radiation. Determining the YORP effect on an asteroid relies on analyzing the relationship between the asteroid's rotation rate and its size and shape, which can be achieved if a significant number of its surface features are tracked over time. Such studies can be made possible with the help of light curves and linear polarization curves, as seen with the asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos. The combination of optical data and YORP data for these asteroids led to a calculation of their shape, size, and rotation period, as well as their surface albedo and phase angle. The linear polarization data in particular helped in filtering out spurious solutions in optical data solutions. The resulting models indicate the YORP effect is active on (1685) Toro and (1620) Geographos, causing a change in their rotation rates over time, as observed with the help of ground-based and space-based observations, as seen with the aid of data from the Akatsuki mission.

We demonstrate that for any compact set $K$ in a torus that isn't a single point, the group of homeomorphisms of the torus which fix points within $K$ also fix them in reverse order forms a group that doesn have a small displacement property. This holds true for any set $K$ consisting of more than one point.

This creation constitutes an implementation of infinite sequence regularity tools, specifically the theorems by Berstel and Reutenauer, and Cauchy's automatic sequence construction, enabling the verification of the regularity of given sequences and determination of their minimal automatic recognition automata.

This paper investigates a complex animal movement pattern called a "puller" hysteresis coexistence, which arises due to an unstable equilibrium point in a system with symmetric repulsive forces from multiple patches. A hidden threshold is discovered that distinguishes the coexistence region from forces that prevent a animal from moving. A new "hidden coexisting puller" data set is created, and a five-neuron artificial neural network is trained to identify the coexistence region from training data. The trained network successfully identifies the coexistence region in unseen test data.

We develop an innovative approach for determining the attainability regions of optimal control problems, particularly those involving discontinuous coefficients and non-convex inputs. Our attainsability region calculation method is second-order accurate, in contrast to existing first-order numerical methods. Our novel technique leverages a discrete approximation of the Cauchy problem associated with a variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation to define the boundary of attainable sets.

The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is characterized by functional regions that are dedicated to processing objects in the visual domain. The mechanism behind these regions remains unclear, particularly with respect to an area known as the animacy arrangement (AA), located between the face and body fields. Some think this area reflects a fundamental characteristic of the objects being processed, whereas others believe it results from a bias towards social objects or is a product of our exposure to the natural world. To test the essential nature ofAA, we used a variety of categorical attributes including quantity, motion, biology, and art, and used both typical and atypical examples within each category.animacy arrangement held up mainly when presented with non-biological categories, but its disappearance during experimental conditions with a lack of typicality or increased familiarity with the social aspect of performance suggested that typicality plays a crucial role in its origin.  A typicality-based computational model effectively replicated our findings, indicating that typicality may be the key factor behind the AA's presence in the ventral temporal cortex.

This research provides a significant improvement in the rate of convergence for the argument of the critical value of the Dirichlet L-function, linked to a specific type of complex quadratic field. As the conductor of this type of field increases, the rate of convergence for the angle is shown to be $O(\log^2 f_L)$ or potentially $O(\log f_L)$, representing a substantial reduction from the previously established $10^{-3}$ fraction of its total angle. Additionally, this result is connected to the distribution of the prime numbers in relation to certain types of mathematical functions and has a corresponding theorem regarding their distribution.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that anticipates outcomes, drawing on the foundational work of Cox and Insall regarding single-quantum system propositional reasoning. Our approach builds on recent single and multi-relationship Hoare calculus for quantum programs. Our work extends these principles to encompass anticipations, drawing on the work of Imramova and Wisniewski. Our formulation of reasoning rules is supported by a connection to single-quantum system reasoning, similar to that of Imramova and Wisniewski. Furthermore, our framework provides an intuition of interference based on the amplitude of a quantum state, and we have demonstrated its practical application in verifying quantum algorithms such as Grover's amplitude amplification and the Bernstein-Vazirans algorithm.

The transmission of airborne pathogens is influenced by individual variations, and in some cases, a small number of highly active carriers can significantly drive the spread of a disease. To better understand and model this phenomenon, particularly in the context of COVID-19, researchers have incorporated "super-spreader" events into an epidemiological framework. The study reveals that high levels of suppression that drive widespread diseases are often linked to a few extreme cases of super-spreading. Consequently, fully eradicating a disease requires not only reducing transmission but also identifying and managing super-spreader events. Additionally, targeting these events by focusing on high-risk settings could prove an effective strategy for controlling the spread of airborne pathogens.

Let topological vector space be denoted as $X$ and a subset $S$ of $X$ with a weakly closed property. This paper investigates the codiskcyclicity and codiskcyclicity with respect to a subset of an operator $T$ on $X$. It establishes that if a collection of operators $\Sigma$ is diskcyclic with respect to $S$ then it is also codiskcyclic with respect to $S$. It further proves that if $\Sigma$ is essential diskcyclic with respect to $S$ then it is essentially codiskcyclic with respect to $S$. It is interesting to note that if $\Sigma$ is weakly diskcyclic with respect to $S$ then it is also weakly codiskcyclic with respect to $S$. It is proposed that the concept of codiskcyclicity can be expanded to include the case where the topological vector space has a locally convex property.

The precision of the vector magnetic field measurement on the Sun has seen significant improvement in recent years, primarily due to advances in instrumentation and the development of more sophisticated inversion techniques. A fundamental challenge in obtaining this data arises from the magnetic fields' weak strength in the photosphere, which makes them difficult to detect through traditional spectrometric methods. As a result, many inversion techniques rely on simplified radiative transfer models that can introduce systematic errors in measured quantities, particularly in regions with higher magnetic field strength. A study investigated the potential for these inversion techniques to produce biased estimates in specific regions, finding that the typical approach known as the Stokes $V$ broadening law underestimates the true distribution of magnetic field strength. This bias leads to the underestimation of $\alpha$ in the strong component and may distort estimates of global properties such as the average helicity and linkage of the vector magnetic field. The study found that using more accurate radiative transfer models can help correct this bias in property estimates.

The Sign Problem, hindering many Monte Carlo simulations in condensed matter and high-energy physics, is addressed by a novel approach using complex-valued neural networks to streamline the partitioning of path integrals.

This research investigates how topological complexity measures, specifically topological entropy and factor complexity, of subshifts change under the morphic images produced by free group free monoids. We establish that a subinjective mapping preserves both topological entropy and factor complexity, implying that if a subshift has finite complexity and is recognized by a mapping of this type, its preimage also has finite complexity. Under certain conditions, if a subshift has zero topological entropy and is recognized by such a mapping, its preimage is uniformly recurrent and also exhibits zero topological entropy. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, a subshift with finite complexity is pre-imageable by a free group mapping if and only if it is compatible with the equivalence relation induced by that mapping. Moreover, we confirm that the topological complexity of a subshift that is invariant under such a mapping is equivalent to the complexity of its set of representative words.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to new tasks without explicit guidance, the capability of generalizing knowledge across different domains is a key area of research in artificial intelligence.
To further explore this phenomenon, we conducted an extensive empirical study and discovered two primary mechanisms underlying it:
1. When knowledge from one task can effectively support another, we observe strong generalization performance even without data.
2. However, in certain cases, the existing knowledge becomes unhelpful, resulting in poorer performance compared to starting fresh.
To capture these phenomena more effectively, we developed a novel unsupervised cross-task learning framework that continuously evaluates the value of existing knowledge and selectively integrates it, we call this framework RETrieval enBaancing Cross-task gEneraIization (REBECI).
Our results show that the two generalization patterns observed are prevalent and that our method, on average, significantly outperforms standard approaches, providing valuable insights for designing more efficient machine learning systems.

This report examines the necessity of hyperparameter optimization in secure deep learning models, which are guaranteed to be private versus those optimized for general performance. Current methodologies focus on individual parameters, ignoring the influence of diverse hyperparameters on security and model efficiency. We investigate four critical hyperparameters - mini-batch optimization, activation function selection, dropout usage, and data normalization - that can impact both the security and performance of these models. Our experiments reveal at least three parameters requiring optimization to achieve security guarantees while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, we identify a significant performance advantage for models with optimized hyperparameters over standard implementations, demonstrating a 5% improvement in accuracy over Mini-Batch Secure Aggregation and achieving parity in security and efficiency with other preprocessing techniques.

This study classify all infinite subsequences of the Cayley boolean structures of the symmetric group $S_n$ that are inclusion dense. Additionally, a specific example is identified that is not considered a subsequence of any infinite Cayley boolean structure of $S_n$.

We present a comprehensive analysis of metallicities for 7354 stars from the APOGEE-2 pilot data set, employing a novel calibration method. This method leverages high-precision metallicities from SDSS and Moeser et al., combined with a customized spectral model, to accurately determine metallicities. This procedure ensures consistency with the original APOGEE scale while offering a wider metallicities range from -5.0 to 0.0. When compared to existing solutions, our method demonstrates superior performance in both categories. Furthermore, we applied this procedure to .050 um/s velocity tensors of these stars, enabling the examination of velocity metallicity space. Enabling the investigation of velocity metallicity space, this space reveals distinct patterns when juxtaposed with PL9 color. Notably, a 90 deg spiral is observable in old stars with [Fe/H] < -1.5, composed of an inner thin disk and an outer thick disk component. In contrast, in a middle metallicities interval (-1.5 < [Fe/H] < -0.5), stars exhibit a mixture of old and intermediate ages. Moreover, we identified a small bulge population with [Fe/H] around -0.8. Overall, this study establishes a precise and reliable metallicity scale for APOGEE-2, facilitating a detailed study of the Milky Way's stellar populations across a broad metallicities range.

A prominent issue during the COVID-19 pandemic was the spread of false health-related information online. This study develops a new mathematical model to analyze the dynamics of rumor propagation, taking into consideration both the external and internal factors that contribute to the sharing of misinformation. The proposed model undergoes a phase analysis, incorporating an exponential growth pattern to assess the impact of content-driven sharing of rumors. A statistical change point detection method is used to identify shifts in daily social media usage and correlates these with inferred basic reproduction numbers of two widely circulated fake news stories. Key variables in the model are estimated using the generalized additive model and confirmed through sensitivity analysis. Comparing daily new infections according to the original and modified models reveals that ignoring the external factors driving the spread of misinformation results in underestimating the number of new cases by up to 13 times. Furthermore, analyzing policy interventions reveals that suppressing the online sharing of rumors could have reduced the cumulative number of people exposed to at most 67 million.

To advance the measurement of external distances, it's crucial to understand the spectral features and evolution of planetary nebulae (PNe). Our knowledge in this area has been primarily developed from extensive surveys of Milky Way galaxies, but these findings may not be directly applicable to other host galaxies due to potential differences in environmental interactions and the statistical properties of supernovae type Ia within them. As a remedy, we are establishing the Fornax3D project, which involves conducting high-resolution spectroscopy of PNe in three key galaxies of the Fornax cluster - SO-1, GC-1, and NGC 3621 - through a combination of previous data and new observations using the VLT. By analyzing these data, we will determine the statistical properties of the PNe and use them as tracers to understand the environment of the galaxies and their intergalactic space. Furthermore, we are developing an artificial intelligence-based classification system for PNe and testing the validity of external distance measurements. In addition to these findings, the PNe data will be compiled into a comprehensive catalog of the three galaxies, facilitating their study in the context of field galaxy research.

Because remote work and online services have become ubiquitous, ensuring the reliability of everyday stream data applications has become an pressing issue. Existing robust stream processing frameworks, adapted from traditional database systems, are capable of providing a stable experience for these applications but at a significant performance cost. In contrast, leading stream processing frameworks exhibit high efficiency but lack the necessary robustness. To address these challenges, we introduce LifeFlow, a robust stream processing engine that can handle regular applications with exceptional performance while offering guaranteed failover for reliable guarantees. LifeFlow incorporates a unique design called "current leader" and leverages existing crash-consistent technologies, including memory and log replication, to minimize robustness' impact on performance. Our findings reveal that LifeFlow can handle the robustness required for failover without significant slowdown. We've observed an approximately 80% reduction in end-to-end latency, an 70% decrease in message processing throughput loss, and an 60% reduction in buffer overflow. LifeFlow's real-world benchmark results show significant improvements over both robust adaptations of MVCC and consistent algorithms.

This research paper provides evidence that certain types of curves, specifically timelike curves within a specific type of space known as a 4-dimensional semi-Euclidean space called $R_4$, under certain conditions related to their geometric properties in this space, can be classified as Bertrand curves based on the characteristics of those properties.

The primary objective of this study is to investigate how modifying the loss function in a deep learning classifier impacts the resulting model's performance. To begin with, standard loss functions commonly employed in the field are briefly reviewed and discussed. Building on this foundation, new loss functions are proposed and proposed to be evaluated. Through extensive experiments, an analysis of the effects loss function modifications have on model accuracy is conducted, utilizing benchmark datasets and referencing prior research findings. The research reveals that the decision to alter the loss function isn't purely random and is influenced by the specific characteristics of the data set in question. Furthermore, a novel, generalizable loss function is developed and found to outperform standard loss functions across a wide range of classification problems.

This research aims to numerically analyze the development of mechanical
microstructures in polymer materials subjected to simultaneous thermal and
mechanical processes.  Strain-induced crystallization, which occurs when
polymers undergo deformation at certain temperatures, can lead to the formation
of mechanical defects such as folds and voids as a result of their viscoelastic
and thermomechanical characteristics.  Understanding these microstructures is
crucial in materials science due to their non-negligible influence on mechanical
performance.  Our simulation model, based on the Strain-induced Crystallization
(SIC) approach, incorporates a Strain Energy Splitting method, a damage evolution
equation, and a temperature field equation to investigate the NA65-TAU test 
simulation.  Although this application was our primary focus, the developed 
framework is applicable to a wide range of problems involving SIC.  The 
results reveal that the simulation captures the primary features observed 
experimentally, and demonstrates the capacity for the simulation model to 
represent the complex mechanical microstructures that arise as a result of 
SIC-induced void and fold interactions.

We analyze a model of a nematic superconductor with a pair-breaking magnetic field applied in the perpendicular direction. A pair-breaking field is strongly dependent on the nematic character due to the magnetization of triplet Cooper pairs with their magnetic moments oriented in the nematic d-wave symmetry. The model is mathematically expressed as a self-consistent equation for the order parameter with its components in the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and a p-x (or p-y) symmetry determined by the external field. Our study involves investigating the susceptibility in the normal state, finding the gap equation's solutions in the superconducting state and analyzing the critical temperature's behavior as it nears the normal state transition with a fixed anomaly parameter.

This article analyzes a shift in time axis in differential continuous phase modulation (CPM) detection and identifies the improved performance of a specific scheme, named offset differential matched filter detection (ODMFD), compared to traditional matched filter detection (MFD). It is demonstrated that CPM's lack of a defined reference phase in match filtering can be addressed in reduced complexity schemes like differential detection by shifting data axis before demodulation. This approach highlights ODMFD's superior performance over conventional matched filter detection (MFD).

A notable feature of the quantum expression for the Bernoulli equation is the emergence of the quantum potential, which is then connected to the compressibility of vacuum in accordance with the Bernoulli's equation of state. This investigation delves into the quantum potential in relation to a thermal system confined within a one-dimensional box. The findings indicate that the quantum potential is directly proportional to the osmotic pressure in accordance with the uncertainty principle. The expression for the quantum potential is derived for multiple systems, including a single particle, two fermions, and a boson, across various temperatures and system sizes. The proportionality between the quantum potential and the compressibility of vacuum is confirmed by verifying the quantum potential at the infinity of the De Broglie pilot wave. The results for both the quantum potential and the compressibility of vacuum are presented in charts for visualization.

Rule-based systems, characterized by a knowledge-based approach, have been extensively utilized in various domains, including natural language processing, due to their simplicity and interpretability. The integration of large language models (LLMs) as rule generators has gained prominence recently. However, a critical limitation of using plain LLMs is their propensity for hallucinations and inconsistencies. In contrast to a desired format of structured knowledge, often represented as a set of condition-action pairs, LLMs may produce knowledge that is ambiguous, contains superfluous information, or is inapplicable in specific scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce ATOMIC, an innovative framework consisting of 3 million knowledge points designed to guide subsequent inference. ATOMIC encompasses three key components that facilitate the utilization of rule-based systems: selection points to determine the applicability of a statement, syntax to unify the format of knowledge, and correction to rectify inaccuracies or incomplete information. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-stage pipeline, which first employs an LLM to generate an initial draft of rules and then refines them through a more accurate but computationally less demanding method. The practical value of ATOMIC is evident in its capacity to enhance the precision of narrative text understanding by 11.1% when compared to a baseline system.

In this study, we adapt Shor's original 1996 quantum algorithm for resolving linear systems of equations, addressing critical limitations that hindered its initial implementation. By addressing stability and precision challenges inherent in the method, we created a revised algorithm suitable for near-term quantum applications, specifically utilizing the IBM's 127-qubit processor, ibm\_grover-127. Dd-ALGO, as our algorithm is named, was evaluated through numerical simulations and demonstrated a precise resolution of challenging test cases. Furthermore, it outperformed the conventional conjugate gradient method when applied to a real-world short-term investment problem.

To improve the accuracy of speech transcription systems, especially with limited data, this study introduces a novel, straightforward multi-modal training approach. The study expresses the text-based input as a probability distribution and establishes a focused region around the target sentence's words. The concept of "bidirectional focus" is introduced to give equal importance to the words preceding and following the target sentence. This method is demonstrated on two tasks, beginning with a simple speech understanding task using auditory and textual inputs. The study easily extends to sequence classification and leverages both focus regions in those cases. The results show that this multi-modal approach outperforms existing techniques and even a powerful baseline in a range of speech transcription tasks. The authors' code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ZehaoWu/BidirectionalFocus.

By analyzing uniform measures on the set of parking functions $\FP_n$, we establish that the positions converge in distribution to a set of independent uniform distributions on the interval $[0,1]$. Moreover, we determine the measure of positions falling within a given subset $A$ of $[0,1]^k$ that remains invariant under transformations by the symmetric group $S_k$. Measurements of tunneling conductance have been made through a gate-controlled NbN nanowire sandwiched between two metallic electrodes in a Josephson tunneling configuration. The results show abrupt changes in coherent quantum interference patterns at phase transitions of the superconducting state from bulk to nanowire. The data do not support the Coulomb obstruction theory as they lack evidence for the onset of single-electron tunneling, likely due to inadequate oxidation of the nanowire that would be necessary for such effects. The study also reveals unusual phase-dependence in the activation energy and optimal conductance in the nanowire, in addition to abrupt loss of Andreev oscillations at a critical thickness at which the nanowire's geometry induces a transition from a 1D to 0D superconductor.

To enhance future scene understanding, a novel framework is proposed that processes video data by dividing it into two distinct representations: visual and event-based. The visual representation captures the future frame and intermediate video segments, while the event-based representation identifies past present-day events and predicts future events. By combining these representations through a fusion mechanism, a comprehensive forecast of the future scene is created. It has been tested and showed superior performance compared to previous methods on the D4W and TUM-RGBD datasets.

Covariance between occupation numbers in different atomic orbitals of a single atom is an key aspect that has been neglected in many simplified quantum chemical calculations that assume covariance effects are insignificant. However, a study of a diverse range of atomic states reveals significant interorbital covariance values and implies that covariance operators could enhance the precision of various performance metrics in a number of atoms.

The Ω-baryon, distinguished by its -3 strangeness value, has long been a theoretically predicted particle that is crucial in the Standard Model of particle physics. Its discovery would be a significant breakthrough in physics. For a considerable time, searches for this particle were confined to experiments at fixed targets, which were limited by background noise. This changed with the rise of particle detectors at colliders, offering much higher search capabilities. The document delves into an examination of the $K^- K^- K^-\Omega^-$ decay process occurring in $\Omega_b^-$ baryon decays, analyzing its physics background, potential, and branching fraction. It is found that $\Omega_b^-$ baryon decays have a minimum width of $1.56 \, \text{mrad}$ for the $K^- K^- K^-\Omega^-$ process.

Recent studies on network models have introduced "well-mixed" subnetworks consisting of randomly connected nodes, and we investigate the epidemiological dynamics of a two-layer network with an airline or bus as a fully interconnected system and individual nodes representing seating positions. A primary contribution of this research is a set of new formulas that derive the basic reproduction number for a wide range of betwixt mixing environments, and we observe from numerical experiments and field data that the model's predictions accurately match the spread of infectious diseases and over-time infection prevalence. The studies have shown that assessing infection prevalence on network models requires more complex modeling than traditional approaches, and well-mixed framework models provide a significant improvement in predictive accuracy compared to conventional approaches that account for contact heterogeneity.

This study explores spin-orbit proximity effects in cobalt layers adjacent to a bismuth interface, revealing that the spin-orbit coupling constant of cobalt can be modified by cobalt thickness reductions from 4 nm to 1 nm, without altering the cobalt's intrinsic properties. The research and theoretical modeling indicate that boundary scattering induced by the heavy-atom effect is responsible for these findings, offering new insights for developing hybrid materials with tailored spin-orbit coupling for various applications.

This research provides analytic solutions for a generalized Mie-type potential within the context of a fractional version of the time-independent Schrödinger equation in $ \alpha $-dimensions. We apply the Jumarie type fractional derivative to a potential that encompasses various physical phenomena, including the Morse, Coulomb, and Hulthén potentials as special cases. By utilizing the generalized series expansion method, we derive solutions and determine the associated energy eigenvalues for the fractional model. Further analysis involves a comparative examination of our findings with previous results. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the potential's physical bounds and present corresponding graphs to facilitate a better understanding of the phenomena under study.

We analyze a form of consistency training that requires a neural network's
output to remain similar to its neighbor's when the latter is a noisy version of
the former. This type of consistency training has been successfully applied to
a wide range of tasks. In this study, we prove that the consistency loss
function controls the Lipschitz constant of a neural network with high
probability, and that this control is linked to the data distribution and the
network's dimensionality. We also demonstrate that adding the consistency loss
function controls the complexity of the network in terms of its Kolmogorov–Taylor
basis functions' norm. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for
why consistency training performs so effectively. Furthermore, this evidence
supports the practice of pretraining neural networks with consistency learning
before they are trained with labeled data. We incorporated this approach into
the current consistency training methods and found that it led to better
performance with less dimensional networks and prevented excessive robustness
in instances of Data Augmentation and Self-supervised Neural Process
Pretraining. This approach did not underperform when compared to the current
state-of-the-art standards in several classified datasets with missing parts.

We investigate the Drell-Yan production of colorless final states in a specific third-generation gauge vector leptoquark model via $u \bar{u} \to \gamma \gamma / \gamma ^{+} \gamma _ { T }$ during proton-proton collisions at high-energy colliders like the LHC and the FCChh. By conducting an in-depth analysis of the NLO QCD corrections to this process using MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, we are able to compare our findings with experimental data from the LHC and provide precise limits on the leptoquark mass based on existing ATLAS measurements, as well as forecast for a muon collider at FCCee.

Radiation exposure during Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging is limited, resulting in images of low quality with high false positive rates. Deep-learning methods have been successful in enhancing low-dose PET images but struggle when faced with images containing severe noise levels outside their training data ranges. This research introduces a novel Out-of-Distribution (OOD) conscious neural network, called Pandapet, to explicitly identify and separate OOD images, preventing them from distorting the model's performance. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not require knowledge of variance in image data and offers an innovative, flexible framework for learning. Experimental results show that our method achieves significant improvements in identifying OOD images and produces more accurate and reliable enhanced images compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

According to Centering Theory, a communicative focus model introduced by Rockwell and Goldman in 1986, the most recent mention in a conversation is considered to have the highest significance. This signifies that a neural coreference resolver should be able to rank a person's most recent mention of an entity higher than external references to the same entity. This research evaluates if centering principles can be applied to the neural coreference task, specifically testing the validity of two centering-based features, including prior mention probability, within a prominent neural coreference method. It is demonstrated that incorporating these features according to the CTR framework can help a 24-million mention dataset's resolver distinguish entity mentions more effectively.

The utilization of WiFi access points for electronic positioning and distance
evaluation has been well-documented. This research focuses on determining the
distance between a device and an access point, expressed as signal-to-noise ratio
(SNR). The paper aims to create a predictive model to estimate distances between
a device and an access point, leveraging supervised machine learning techniques.
The paper leverages the extensive dataset from the IEEE 802.11 directed trilateration
evaluation method and employs a uniform approach to determine and validate model
accuracy using the same test and training sets at various locations. The paper
reveals that the optimal results can be achieved through the use of artificial
neural networks, yielding accurate distance estimations between a device and an
access point, with mean absolute errors of 0.67 meters, 0.65 meters, and 0.63
meters at three distinct locations, respectively. The paper provides a comprehensive
analysis of its findings and results.

The beam fragmentation instability poses a significant risk of reducing the overall efficiency of energy recovery linacs, particularly when operating in a open configuration. To improve performance, it is crucial to develop a comprehensive understanding of how this phenomenon manifests in both open and closed configurations, with a view towards optimizing system performance. This paper presents an analysis of research findings and identifies gaps in knowledge with the aim of filling these configurations dependence data gaps. By presenting experimental results, it becomes evident that regenerative beam fragmentation instability exhibits similar characteristics across both open and closed configurations, thus enabling the existing mitigation strategies to be effectively applied in both scenarios.

The paper presents the one-loop CE vertex for two gluons with a color factor of zero in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, utilizing the BKPV algorithm and the color decomposition of amplitude. This is achieved through a more efficient method of extracting the required coefficient, involving the extraction of the appropriate partial amplitude from a $\mathcal{D}$-function. The results obtained are verified through explicit computation of the relevant six-gluon amplitude.

This research builds upon the concept of molten polymer bristles with arbitrarily shaped backing plates, where individual polymer chains may become disorganized in a molten state beyond a certain distance from the plate's surface. It finds that, for viscoelastic polymers in a molten state at the tip, exclusion regions can be ignored for elongated shapes but must be accounted for for simpler shapes like squares and triangles. The size of these exclusion regions is influenced by the shape of the plate, the number of polymer chains, and how much the plate is stretched. It provides formulas to estimate the number of chains in a annular region where the molten state occurs, showing that for very stretched plates, this region's shape can be considered an ellipse whose dimensions are directly related to the plate's elongation. Moreover, this study establishes a relationship between the placement of chains at arbitrary positions on the plate and the overall drag force experienced by the plate as it moves through a pool of viscoelastic fluid.

A subset of vertices in a graph G is considered deterministic if, when combined with their neighboring distances to the subset, they provide a distinct measurement for all other vertices in the graph. The smallest possible size of such a deterministic subset is known as the minimum metric dimension of the graph. This concept is important in various applications, including network communication systems. The variant of the metric dimension under consideration here is called the shortened metric dimension, which occurs when the deterministic subset of vertices is combined with a set of edge-to-vertex associations that contribute to the unique distance measurements. The article considers the determination of the shortened metric dimension for several types of graphs, including directed and undirected cycles, complete multipartite graphs, and their line graphs.

A notable issue with astronomical images is source variability, which hinders the effectiveness of current catalogs and maps that are widely used in research and educational purposes. A new method is proposed to address this issue by utilizing machine learning, specifically a random forest model, to estimate the probability of sources changing over time from astronomical data spanning more than a decade from the Fermi-LAT. This model identifies variable sources with higher accuracy compared to previous methods and ranks individual telescopes' ability to detect a source's variability. A new metric is proposed to measure variability and is demonstrated by applying the model to well-known variable sources like V444 Pyx and Markarier 447.

A serial dictatorship mechanism is considered the best possible method to prevent manipulation in a general setting when agents are required to rank available options. To improve efficiency, we introduce a family of mechanisms that can outperform serial dictatorships in certain efficiency measures when the available options are discrete. These mechanisms are proven to be robust, as they satisfy the same manipulability constraints as agents with limited cognitive abilities, namely the 2-limit condition. Given the extensive prevalence of ranked data generated by such algorithms, we establish their applicability and provide a precise characterization of how they can be utilized. Furthermore, we discover and define the 2-limit condition as the most restrictive condition that ensures growth in the size of the set of available options when the size of this set increases. This in-turn allows us to establish that any efficient mechanism that is invariant to the size of this set can be modeled as a combination of a limited number of matching algorithms. These mechanisms are shown to be the only class of mechanisms that can be utilized when the available options have a finite size.

This research paper examines data from the Pan-STARRS1 Optical Survey, specifically the Point Source Catalog, released in 2017, with a focus on identifying and characterizing binary asteroids. Initial steps involved filtering the asteroid catalog for suitable targets for long-term orbital analysis of binary systems. A method was developed and applied to 305 such targets, utilizing the light curve database, resulting in 29 exhibits of photometric variability indicative of binary configurations. These examples are explored in detail, considering factors such as rotation periods and orbital characteristics. Notably, a new record for the slowest rotation period observed in an asteroid was discovered, at 2246 Thebe with a period of 7.62 days. Furthermore, the study highlights the significance of binary asteroids that exhibit long rotation periods, plotting them against those with single-period light curves to discern patterns.

Large-scale network data has become a significant tool for investigating social network effects and the application of econometric methods. We investigate a linear regression model with an explanatory variable represented by a network matrix, utilizing conventional ordinary least squares estimation. Our primary contribution involves proving consistency and central limit theorems for the model's coefficients and standard errors under minimal regularity assumptions, providing standard statistical inference methods and enabling assessment of theoretically predicted network standard errors. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical relevance of a partially linear framework by applying it to analyze peer influence within online peer-to-peer file-sharing networks. Our results indicate that peer influence is predominantly positive and standard errors can be reliably estimated based on networks alone.

This study develops a modified version of the Leibniz Theorem that is specific to the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative, addressing the limitations of the original theorem, which is limited to constant order cases. To demonstrate the applicability of our fractional variant, we examine it in relation to the product rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative, yielding several novel results. Furthermore, by iterating the product rule, we derive a corresponding variation of the Leibniz Theorem on the interaction between the variable-order fractional integral and derivative operator and its inverse, offering novel insights into this complex mathematical domain.

Training a reinforcement learning agent to effectively communicate and
navigates the same environment as a human requires overcoming the challenge of
aligning the two different objectives. The AI Dungeon Alignment project tackles
this issue by learning to play Dungeons and Dragons alongside a human player, with
the goal of creating an AI that can engage in meaningful conversation and guide
the game's progression like a friendly dungeon master. To evaluate this, we
developed several novel metrics, and with those, we demonstrate effective training
of an GPT-3-based AI dungeon master that mirrors the behavior of a human player
